children.text:
I should add that Llama.app and Unsloth Studio provide OpenAI-compatible API endpoints (both use Llama.cpp as their backend).

https://llama.app/docs/api

https://unsloth.ai/docs/new/studio#unsloth-as-an-api-endpoin...

The choice of model could be up to the user, depending on the available RAM on their M class Mac. Newer and bigger usually being smarter.

Llama.app/.cpp and Unsloth Studio on Mac already provide guidance to pick the optimal model for the available memory, all model wheights hosted by huggingface. Both apps can use the local huggingface model cache locally.

If you make it configurable, the user could also run a separate machine with an NVidia card and Linux to serve tokens on the LAN. Or use OpenRouter or any other cloud hosted model offering (DeepSeek, Z.ai, etc.).

Thank you so much!

Most daily commands like launching and moving around sites/apps happen without AI, but I agree with the privacy concern and will definitely look into utilizing local AI.

Smaller models, like Haiku, I have found to already struggle during multi-step tasks, so I expect local model capabilities to reduce performance further.

I'll look into how OOMU splits their work up, but what local model would you suggest starting with?

This looks and works great, super impressed. This is what Siri/Apple AI should be like.

One concern I have is about sending private info to Anthropic. So it would be great to have the option to use local AI.

Local options should support the OpenAI API that seemingly is the standard for these connections, as provided by Llama.app and Unsloth Studio for example. That way one could run against a local model and keep personal information private.

That of course begs the question if a local model is smart enough for the tasks at hand.

I'm also trying out OOMU, a similar but closed source personal assistant app for MacOS. It emphasizes privacy with local models, and even has an 'Airplane' mode. The app has a built in llama.cpp server and uses Gemma-4-4B, their own router model plus a vision model.

children.text: Please make this more generic, using the OpenAI API standard with model discovery. That way it works against a bare Llama.cpp instance out of the box, the local inference server that many others wrap around (like Ollama and LM Studio).

Thanks! I believe I can add Deepseek support pretty easily. Atticus runs on Claude Code, and Claude Code can point to any server that uses Claude's API. DeepSeek has one so I added a Custom server option in Settings > Intelligence > Custom server. Put in https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic, your DeepSeek key, and deepseek-chat as the model. Same thing works for Ollama or LM Studio.

One thing is that DeepSeek's API doesn't take images, so anything where Atticus has to look at your screen won't work on it. Opening apps, music, web stuff, and shell commands are fine. I'll push this in an upcoming update.

source.text:
Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus.

Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it.

The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev.

Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent.

To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you.

To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action.

Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you.

To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS.

Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!
source.title: Show HN: Atticus – Hold-to-talk voice assistant for macOS that runs on Claude -p
